text.p: Monaco, despite coach Jean Tigana's words of caution, look set to lift the French league title for the sixth time after brushing aside their closest challengers Paris Saint-Germain.

"I remind you that not long ago Paris had an eight-point lead and that there are still 14 matches to play," warned coach Jean Tigana after Monaco's 2-0 win over PSG on Sunday night put them seven points clear.
"It is in fact a very small step towards the title. It could all be in doubt again very quickly. We're going to be pressed with the UEFA Cup as well. The championship is not done."
The figures for the last nine seasons in a row, however, show that the match between the top two sides in the second half of the season held the key to the outcome of the championship.
On every occasion since Bordeaux beat Marseille on their way to the title in 1987, the team that won the top-of-the-table clash, home or away, went on to be crowned champions.

Monaco were held in check for an hour by PSG before breaking the deadlock when France goalkeeper Bernard Lama failed to control a header by midfielder Sylvain Legwinski and allowed the home side to take the lead.
The goal, although lucky, was just reward for the more ambitious side, who had already come close to scoring twice in a tight match, while PSG did not create a single clear-cut chance.
Tigana, not content to play for a draw which would still have suited his team, sent on a third forward in Nigeria's Victor Ikpeba on the hour -- four mintues before the goal.

Seven minutes later the quick Ikpeba fed the equally fast Anderson from deep in his own half with a well weighted ball that beat the PSG offside trap and the Brazilian raced through to put the result beyond doubt.
"He (Ikpeba) gave depth to our game," Tigana said.
Scot John Collins, who made way for Ikpeba, praised Tigana for the courage of his convictions.
"The coach's decision was courageous to change tactics at that moment. It could have failed but it paid off," he said.
Statistics also show that Monaco have scored a majority of their 42 goals in 24 games in the last quarter.
PSG's best spell tends to be in the 15 to 20 minutes before halftime, but they were unable to profit from a solid first half in which the Monaco defence kept a tight rein on their forwards.
Lama said: "The match summed up our season. We do fine in the first half and fall away in the second."
"We made the difference physically," Monaco defender Emmanuel Petit said.
PSG, bowing to the inevitable, are now talking about second place, which from this year also means a place in the European Champions' League, while brushing aside suggestions of a crisis.
"We must consolidate our second place, we're not going to talk about anything else," said PSG chief executive Michel Denisot.
Brazilian coach Ricardo, who had his offer of resignation turned down by Denisot after the 6-1 mauling by Juventus in the European Super Cup 12 days ago, denied he would quit.
"This is different. I still have faith. Each time we lose it's not going to be the same story as after Juve," he said.

PSG's Brazilian midfielder Leonardo, the key player when they recovered from a previous poor spell in October, was a peripheral figure just back from injury and weakened by illness earlier in the week.
Defender Paul Le Guen was looking no further than PSG's next league match at home to lowly Cannes.
"We're disappointed. We'll need courage at the Parc des Princes on Saturday," he said.
PSG's last home games have been so poor they have caused a schism between the team and the majority of their supporters.
They have not won in their last three league games at home, including a 2-1 defeat by relegation candidates Nancy last month, before the crash against Juventus.
